name: How do you match new custom cabinets to existing trim and millwork?

mainEntity.name: What is the process for matching cabinet color, sheen, and wood tone to existing baseboards, doors, and built-ins in an older home?
mainEntity.text: What is the process for matching cabinet color, sheen, and wood tone to existing baseboards, doors, and built-ins in an older home?

acceptedAnswer.text: In older Los Angeles homes, existing trim and millwork often have aged differently from newer cabinetry, so the goal is usually a visual match, not an exact chemical duplicate. Start by identifying whether the existing surfaces are painted, stained, glazed, or clear-coated. Then compare sheen, grain pattern, and undertone in both daylight and artificial light. A skilled finish shop will make spray-outs or sample boards before final production and may build custom stain or paint formulas to get closer to the existing look. If the original wood has yellowed or darkened, account for that aging rather than copying the current color blindly. For the most cohesive result, coordinate cabinet doors, crown, baseboards, and hardware together. If an exact match is critical, ask whether the shop can refinish adjacent trim or create a transition detail so the difference looks intentional instead of accidental.
acceptedAnswer.description: Matching new cabinets to existing trim starts with identifying the wood species, stain base, paint formula, and sheen level already in the home. The best cabinet makers create sample boards, test color in the room, and adjust for aging, oxidation, and light exposure. Perfect matches are difficult, but close visual coordination is usually possible with custom finish work.
